**On Lichen**

There is a boulder in a field I used to pass, and on its north face there was a patch of lichen the color of old mustard. It was about the size of a dinner plate. I never thought much about it until someone told me that the map lichens on rock—the ones that look like flaking yellow paint—grow at roughly a millimeter a year, sometimes less. That dinner plate, then, had been forming since before the field was fenced, before the road was paved, before anyone in the nearest town could remember. It was older than the oaks along the fence line. It was, in a quiet way, one of the oldest living things I had ever put my hand on, and I had been walking past it as though it were a stain.

That's the first thing lichen teaches you: your sense of scale is wrong. Not wrong in the cosmic way that stars and geologic time are wrong, where the numbers get so big they stop meaning anything. Wrong in a domestic way. Something on a rock beside a footpath is keeping a calendar you can't read.

The second thing is stranger. For a long time lichens were classified as plants—odd plants, plants without roots or leaves, but plants. Then in the 1860s a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener looked closely and proposed that a lichen wasn't one organism at all. It was a fungus wrapped around a colony of algae, or sometimes cyanobacteria. The fungus builds the structure and holds water and anchors to the rock; the algae photosynthesize and feed the fungus sugar. Neither could do, alone, what they do together. The scientific establishment hated this. It offended the tidy notion that a species is a single thing with a single lineage. Schwendener was mocked for years. The word "symbiosis" had to be invented, in part, to describe what he'd seen.

Now we know it's even messier than he thought. Many lichens turn out to contain a second fungus, a yeast, tucked into the outer layer, and nobody noticed for a century and a half because nobody thought to look. There are bacteria in there too, doing things we don't fully understand. A lichen is less an organism than a settlement—a small, durable town that has decided, collectively, to live on a rock.

I find I keep returning to that. We have this deep intuition that a living thing should have edges. Here is the cat; here is not-the-cat. Here is you; here is the world. Lichen just doesn't respect it. Ask "what is this" and the honest answer is "a relationship." The relationship is the thing. It has a color and a shape and it can be scraped off with a knife, but if you try to point at the individual, your finger passes through.

They are also absurdly tough. Lichens grow in Antarctica, on the insides of rocks in the Negev, on the roofs of cathedrals and the sides of gravestones and the bark of trees in downtown parking lots. They've been sent into orbit, exposed to vacuum and unfiltered solar radiation for a year and a half, and brought back alive. When conditions are bad, they simply stop. They dry to a crust, metabolism near zero, and wait. When rain comes they reinflate within minutes and pick up where they left off. There's a kind of patience in that which I don't think humans are built to feel, only to admire from outside.

And yet they're fragile in the ways that matter to us. Lichens absorb everything from the air—they have no roots, no soil to buffer them—so they're exquisitely sensitive to pollution. Cities in the industrial era were "lichen deserts"; you could map sulfur dioxide by walking outward from the center and noting where the first grey rosettes appeared on the trees. When air quality laws came in, the lichens came back, slowly, in the order of their tolerances. They are one of the few indicators of environmental health that doesn't require an instrument. You just look at the bark.

I like that they've been useful to people in small, specific ways. Reindeer eat them through the Arctic winter. Orchil, a purple dye, came from a Mediterranean lichen and colored Roman cloth. Litmus—the actual litmus of litmus paper—is a lichen extract. Some Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest baked a black tree lichen into cakes. None of this is grand. Lichen doesn't feed nations or build empires. It's the kind of thing that mattered to a household, a season, a person who knew where to look.

There's a passage in a book by Kimmerer, the botanist, where she describes learning that in Potawatomi, the word for lichen is something like "the ones who take care of the rock" or the ones the rock and the tree share. I may be misremembering the exact phrasing, but the point held: a language that categorizes by relationship arrives, without a microscope, at the same conclusion Schwendener was ridiculed for. It seems worth pausing on. There are things you can see more clearly if you start by assuming the world is made of arrangements rather than objects.

I don't want to make lichen into a metaphor. It's too easy, and lichen deserves better than to be a lesson about cooperation stenciled onto an office wall. It isn't cooperating in any sense it would recognize. The fungus is arguably farming the algae; the algae, if they could opine, might call it captivity. The point isn't that nature is kind. The point is that the categories we bring to it—individual, species, plant, animal, one, many—are ours, and the world is under no obligation to fit them. Sometimes it does, mostly, and we get lucky. Sometimes there's a mustard-colored patch on a boulder that has been quietly failing to fit for six hundred years.

I went back to that field once, later, and the rock was still there and so was the lichen. Same size, as far as I could tell. It had not noticed me leaving, or returning. That seemed correct.
